item.title: Volker Turk's term as UN human rights chief extended despite US warnings. [ dawn ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

item.title: Does the government have a concrete plan for child safety?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

Last month, in my opinion article, “ Child Safety: Beyond Ideological Polarization ,” published in the Dhaka Tribune, I argued that the sexual abuse of children -- including cases occurring within madrasa settings -- is fundamentally a structural governance challenge rooted in weak accountability mechanisms, regulatory failures, and institutional neglect. The urgency of this argument has become even more evident in recent days. Disturbing content has been circulating on TikTok, featuring madrasa teachers openly sexualizing and objectifying their child students. Accompanied by provocative comments, this trend reveals a deeper social crisis: The normalization of predatory attitudes toward children and the total absence of effective preventive safeguards. It forces us to confront an uncomfortable question: Why do these educational institutions continue to fail to ensure child safety, and why does the state allow it? To answer these questions, we must look beyond surface-level moral failings and examine the institutional architecture within which these abuses occur. Bangladesh’s response to child protection crises remains trapped in a reactive cycle. After every tragedy, public anger intensifies, demands for justice peak, and political leaders offer swift sympathy. Following the heartbreaking Ramisa case, the prime minister’s visit to the victim's family and commitment to justice provided necessary, immediate reassurance. Such gestures matter, but they cannot substitute for the institutional systems required to prevent abuse before it occurs. Before the election, the prime minister repeatedly assured the public, " I have a plan ” for the nation. We must now ask for the procedural details of the plan regarding the protection of children. We can no longer afford institutional silence, nor can we accept abstract promises. The current crisis demands a coordinated national response. The government should initiate immediate cross-sector collaboration to develop a concrete, actionable child protection roadmap. This roadmap cannot remain a policy document alone; it must address the deep, internal layers of madrasa management -- including labour standards, teacher residency rules, child protection training, independent monitoring, complaint mechanisms, and external oversight. Most importantly, the roadmap must answer practical questions: How will children be protected tomorrow? How will the educational institutions be monitored? What mechanisms will ensure absolute accountability? A plan on paper is not a plan in practice. The true measure of leadership is not how effectively it responds to public outrage after harm occurs, but whether it builds institutions capable of preventing abuse in the first place. Our children deserve more than sympathy after they suffer; they deserve a system designed to protect them before tragedy strikes. Aisha Siddika is a PhD Candidate at McMaster University, Canada. She can be reached at: asiddika@alumni.uwo.ca.

item.title: Citizens should not be forced to do the government’s work. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B

We must marvel at and admire the residents of the Sreepur upazila in Gazipur. Faced with two decades of waterlogging, blocked drains, and official indifference, they came together, pooled their own money, and built a functional drainage system themselves. This is a testament to community spirit, resilience, and the determination of ordinary citizens who have stood up and refused to live indefinitely with a problem that should have been solved long ago. With that said, let us be clear: This is not how a functioning system is supposed to work. Citizens should not have to become engineers, fundraisers, and municipal workers just to secure basic urban services. The fact that residents had to take matters into their own hands is not a sign of empowerment but rather a sign of institutional failure. That this has been going on for decades where Sreepur has lived with stagnant water, damaged roads, mosquito infestations, and the daily indignity of a problem that no authority seemed willing to fix is simply unacceptable. Their initiative deserves praise, but it also demands introspection. When citizens are forced to build their own infrastructure, it shows just how lacking the governance, accountability, and service delivery truly is. Bangladesh’s urban future cannot depend on communities solving structural problems on their own. Drainage, waste management, roads, water supply -- these are some of the core responsibilities of municipal authorities. When these systems break down, the consequences ripple across public health, mobility, and quality of life. The Sreepur residents have shown what collective action can achieve. It is time now for the authorities to show that they have learned from this and not just offer praise from the sidelines for citizens doing their jobs. They must ensure that no community is left to fend for itself for decades. They must respond faster, plan better, and maintain essential infrastructure. To reiterate, this is unquestionably a positive story. But it should never have been necessary.

item.title: Stopping preventable accidents from claiming more lives. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B

As the world observes World Drowning Prevention Day today, the theme "Unite to turn the tide" is especially relevant for Bangladesh, where drowning remains one of the leading causes of death among young children. Every year, thousands of lives are cut short by drowning -- a tragedy that is both devastating and, in most cases, entirely preventable. The scale of the challenge cannot be ignored: Bangladesh records an estimated 18,000 drowning deaths annually, including around 11,000 children under the age of five. The World Health Organization's call to reduce drowning deaths by 35% by 2035 through coordinated action should, therefore, serve as a rallying cry for policymakers, communities, and families alike. This is not merely a public health concern but a national development issue that robs families of their futures and communities of their youngest members. Many of these deaths occur in rural settings where ponds, canals, and other open water bodies are an unavoidable part of daily life, yet basic water safety measures remain inadequate. What makes this crisis particularly heartbreaking is that proven interventions already exist. Community-based childcare, swimming and water safety lessons, barriers around hazardous water bodies, and greater public awareness have all demonstrated their effectiveness in reducing drowning deaths. The challenge lies not in discovering new solutions but in implementing existing ones -- consistently and at scale. It should be understood that preventing drowning cannot be the responsibility of a single ministry or organization. Schools, local governments, healthcare providers, development partners, civil society, and parents all have critical roles to play. Bangladesh has shown that it can mobilize national efforts to tackle pressing public health challenges, and child drowning most certainly deserves the same level of urgency. If we truly wish to turn the tide, we must transform awareness into sustained action, so that no family has to endure the loss of a child to a preventable accident.
